$comment: The expected answer for the test-design behavioral eval, and the file the agent must never see.
Two fixture sets, each one epic document and each its own case. The seeded set carries five
material risks the epic actually supports and four plausible risks it rules out in as many words.
The clean set carries a feature whose genuine risk set is small, which is what stops recall alone
from rewarding a run that reports everything it can think of.
GROUNDING IS A SUBSTRING TEST, NOT A JUDGMENT
Every material risk names the sentence of the epic that supports it in `groundingQuote`, and every
unsupported risk names the sentence that rules it out in `exclusionQuote`. --validate-only checks
each quote is present in the epic it names, with runs of whitespace collapsed on both sides so a
quote that spans a wrapped line still resolves. A fixture claiming the description supports a risk
the description never mentions fails before a model call is spent.
A reported risk row matches a declared risk when its category is one the risk admits and every
group in `anyOf` has at least one token present in the row's description, case-insensitively. The
groups are an AND of ORs on purpose: one distinctive word is a coincidence and two are a claim.
Material risks are matched first and a matched row is consumed, so a row that names a real risk in
words that also appear in an exclusion is never counted twice.
SEVERITY RANKS CONSTRAIN PAIRS, NOT LEVELS
`severityRank` is an ordering and not a priority. Priority is a separate judgment the workflow
makes from business impact, user reach and workaround availability, which the risk score informs
and does not determine; `resources/knowledge/test-priorities-matrix.md` states that directly and
`resources/knowledge/probability-impact.md` repeats it. Asserting an absolute priority per risk
would measure this fixture's opinion rather than the workflow's rule, so what is checked instead is
that every pair of risks whose ranks are strictly ordered carries priorities in the same order.
Equal ranks constrain nothing and produce no pair.
PROVENANCE
The six categories, the 1-3 probability and impact scales and the P x I score are the workflow's
own, read from steps-c/step-03-risk-and-testability.md section 2 and from the two knowledge
fragments it names. The five test levels are the four steps-c/step-04-coverage-plan.md section 1
declares plus Integration, which resources/knowledge/test-levels-framework.md treats as a first
class level throughout. Both epics were written for this corpus and describe no real system.
EVERY SET DECLARES A CEILING
`maxRisks` bounds how many risks a run may report, and it is on both sets. It was on the clean
control alone, which left over-reporting on the seeded set unbounded: four risks this fixture never
anticipated could be appended to an otherwise correct run and every threshold still passed, because
precision counts only the rows matching a risk the epic rules out in as many words. The seeded
ceiling is 8 against 5 material risks, which leaves room for a real risk this fixture did not
foresee and stops a register that lists everything.

materialRisks.summary: The outbound queue holds a card reference and a billing address unencrypted on the device.
materialRisks.groundingQuote: It holds the full order payload, including the customer's stored card reference and billing address, and it is not encrypted at rest.
materialRisks.exampleDescription: The outbound queue is stored unencrypted on the device, so anyone reaching the local file can read the stored card reference.

materialRisks.summary: Two offline edits to one work order silently overwrite each other, because the server orders by arrival and checks no version.
materialRisks.groundingQuote: The server applies queued edits in the order they arrive and performs no version check and no timestamp check, so a later arrival overwrites an earlier one
materialRisks.exampleDescription: Concurrent offline edits to the same work order overwrite each other on sync, because the server applies queued edits by arrival with no version check.

materialRisks.summary: A payload the server will never accept is retried forever with no backoff, cap or dead-letter path.
materialRisks.groundingQuote: There is no backoff, no attempt cap, and no dead-letter path
materialRisks.exampleDescription: A rejected payload is retried forever with no backoff and no attempt cap, so one bad item loops until the application is killed.

materialRisks.summary: A full day's backlog of 2,000 queued items has to finish syncing within 30 seconds on mid-range hardware.
materialRisks.groundingQuote: requires a full backlog of that size to finish syncing within 30 seconds of regaining connectivity
materialRisks.exampleDescription: A 2000 item backlog may not finish syncing inside the 30 second budget on the mid-range hardware the fleet carries.

materialRisks.summary: The feature ships on for everyone with no flag, so recovery costs a store review of one to three days.
materialRisks.groundingQuote: There is no feature flag, no staged rollout, and no way to disable it without shipping a new build
materialRisks.exampleDescription: There is no feature flag, so a bad release cannot be turned off without shipping a new store build.

unsupportedRisks.summary: A card-processing failure. The epic does not call the billing service and does not change when it charges.
unsupportedRisks.exclusionQuote: the existing billing service charges the stored card reference on its own nightly schedule, and this epic does not touch it, call it, or change when it runs
unsupportedRisks.exampleDescription: The payment gateway is unavailable when the queue uploads, so the customer is never charged for the work.

unsupportedRisks.summary: One organization reading another's orders. Each installation has its own database and shares no storage.
unsupportedRisks.exclusionQuote: one customer organization per installation, with its own database and its own application servers
unsupportedRisks.exampleDescription: A queued order from one organization could be applied to another organization's data, so tenant isolation has to be proven.

unsupportedRisks.summary: A browser or accessibility regression. The client is a native application with no browser surface.
unsupportedRisks.exclusionQuote: There is no browser surface and no web view in this epic
unsupportedRisks.exampleDescription: The order screen has to stay usable with a screen reader and has to render correctly in every supported browser.

unsupportedRisks.summary: A residency or GDPR exposure. Residency is enforced by a routing layer this epic does not modify.
unsupportedRisks.exclusionQuote: Data residency is unchanged and is enforced by the platform's regional routing layer, which this epic does not modify.
unsupportedRisks.exampleDescription: Queued order data could leave its jurisdiction before it is uploaded, which is a GDPR and data residency exposure.

unsupportedRisks.summary: Losing or corrupting stored data. The change opens the settings store read-only and writes nothing.
unsupportedRisks.exclusionQuote: The settings store is opened read-only for this field, so no order, queue entry or setting can be altered or lost by it.
unsupportedRisks.exampleDescription: Reading the settings store could corrupt the stored record and drop a queued entry.

unsupportedRisks.summary: Exposing data to someone who should not see it. The value is the device's own timestamp shown to its holder.
unsupportedRisks.exclusionQuote: it is shown to the person holding the device, so the change exposes nothing to anyone who could not already see it, and it adds no personal data to the screen
unsupportedRisks.exampleDescription: The sync timestamp could expose sensitive personal data to an unauthorized person with access to the screen.

unsupportedRisks.summary: A performance regression. One local key lookup on a screen that is already open, with no network call.
unsupportedRisks.exclusionQuote: The single local key lookup runs on a screen that is already open, so the screen's existing render budget is unchanged.
unsupportedRisks.exampleDescription: The extra read could slow the home screen render and degrade startup latency.

unsupportedRisks.summary: An unrecoverable rollout. The row ships behind an existing flag the release process already toggles.
unsupportedRisks.exclusionQuote: an existing feature flag the release process already toggles per organization, so it can be turned off without a new build
unsupportedRisks.exampleDescription: The new row cannot be disabled without a new build, so a bad rollout has no kill switch.
